title: Belief Systems, Art, and Imperial Legitimacy
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: In the 1570s the Mughal emperor Akbar built the Ibadat Khana, or 'House of Worship,' and invited religious scholars of every faith — Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, and Christian — to debate before him. Akbar concluded that no single religion held all truth and promoted a policy of sulh-i-kull, 'peace with all.'

In the land-based empires, religion was never just a private matter. It was a tool of power and legitimacy, an inspiration for monumental art, and frequently a cause of war, both between empires and within them.

Religious legitimacy was perhaps the most important glue holding the land-based empires together. Rulers presented their authority as chosen or blessed by the divine, so that disobedience became not just treason but blasphemy.

The Ottoman sultan eventually claimed the title of caliph, casting himself as the political successor to Muhammad and protector of all Sunni Muslims. This religious claim was a basis of his legitimacy.

The Safavid shahs claimed religious authority as champions of Twelver Shia Islam, with some claiming descent from the Shia imams. Their identity as defenders of Shiism legitimized their rule and distinguished them from the Sunni Ottomans.

In China, emperors ruled under the ancient concept of the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that Heaven granted the right to rule to a just dynasty and could withdraw it from an unjust one. It was the religious-philosophical basis of Chinese imperial legitimacy.

European kings such as Louis XIV of France invoked the divine right of kings, the claim that royal authority came directly from God. Like the caliphate and the Mandate of Heaven, it tied the ruler to the divine to justify obedience.

Rulers reinforced their legitimacy by building on a colossal scale, turning architecture into propaganda. Monumental religious and royal buildings were designed to awe subjects and broadcast the ruler's wealth, faith, and divine favor.
The Ottomans, through the architect Sinan, raised the magnificent Suleymaniye Mosque dominating Istanbul's skyline. It was a monument to Ottoman power and Sunni Islam.
The Safavids transformed their capital Isfahan into one of the world's most beautiful cities, crowned by stunning blue-tiled mosques. Isfahan displayed Safavid wealth and Shia devotion.

The Taj Mahal is a dazzling white marble tomb that the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built in the mid-1600s for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is at once a love story, a masterpiece blending Islamic, Persian, and Indian art, and an advertisement of Mughal wealth and devotion.

Read as historical evidence, the Taj Mahal reveals the vast strength of the Mughal economy (only enormous tax revenue and labor could build it), the Islamic religious basis of the dynasty's legitimacy (a domed tomb with Quranic calligraphy), and the cultural fusion of Mughal society (Persian, Islamic, and Indian artistic traditions).

The Sunni Ottomans and the Shia Safavids were both political rivals and religious enemies, each regarding the other's Islam as heretical. This sectarian hostility fueled repeated wars and fixed a long Sunni-Shia frontier through the Middle East.

At the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514, the gun-and-cannon-equipped Sunni Ottomans crushed the Shia Safavids. It demonstrated the importance of gunpowder and hardened the Sunni-Shia divide that still shapes Middle Eastern politics today.

The Mughal emperor Akbar pursued religious tolerance: he abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, included Hindus in his government, married a Rajput princess, and promoted 'peace with all' (sulh-i-kull). This inclusion helped hold his Hindu-majority empire together.

The later Mughal emperor Aurangzeb (reigned 1658–1707) reversed Akbar's tolerance, embracing a stricter Sunni orthodoxy and reimposing the jizya. His policies alienated Hindus, Sikhs, and the Maratha confederacy, sparking rebellions that helped weaken the empire.

The contrast between Akbar and Aurangzeb shows that religious tolerance tended to stabilize a diverse empire, while enforced religious uniformity tended to provoke resistance. Religious policy directly affected imperial stability.

Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak around 1500 in the Punjab, drew on both Hindu and Islamic ideas to form a distinct new religion emphasizing one God and human equality. It is a key example of religious syncretism, the blending of faiths.

The Protestant Reformation, launched by Martin Luther in 1517, split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant branches and triggered a century of religious wars in Europe. It is part of the same global story of religion dividing societies in this era.

The land-based empires shared deep similarities: all expanded using gunpowder weapons, all built centralized states with recruited or merit-based elite officials and tax systems, and all used religion to legitimize the ruler and monumental architecture to display power. They were parallel solutions to building a vast centralized state.

The land-based empires differed in religion (Sunni Ottomans, Shia Safavids, Mughals ruling a Hindu majority) and in tolerance (Akbar's inclusion versus Aurangzeb's orthodoxy), as well as in their elite institutions (devshirme versus ghulams versus the Confucian exam system). Mughal tolerance suited rule over a non-Muslim majority.

A strong comparison of the land empires works across three axes: military (how they expanded — gunpowder), administrative (how they governed — elite corps, taxation, bureaucracy), and religious (how they legitimized rule and handled diversity). Comparing on multiple axes and explaining why differences existed earns the most points.

The religious decisions of these empires still shape the world: Shah Ismail's making Persia a Shia state set Iran on a path it follows today, the Ottoman-Safavid wars hardened the enduring Sunni-Shia divide, and Mughal Hindu-Muslim tensions echo into the 1947 partition of India and Pakistan.

While the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal land empires poured their energy into conquering and governing contiguous territory, Atlantic European states turned toward the oceans to build maritime empires. The contrast between the land empire and the sea empire is a master key to understanding how the modern world took shape.
